challenges.title: Rush Job
challenges.brief: When the cell is pushed to rush an order, the arm moves fast while a person is still close by, and the shipped rules never stop it in time. Change the limits so every harm is stopped, without stopping the cell for no reason.
challenges.hint: Harm happens when speed and closeness combine. A limit that acts earlier on either one closes the gap.
challenges.lesson: Each limit looked reasonable alone, but harm came from two readings that were each just inside their limits. Good profiles set limits for the combinations that cause harm, which is why thresholds are tested against scenarios and never picked one at a time.

challenges.title: Noisy Floor
challenges.brief: The shipped rules catch every harm on the humanoid floor, and they stop the robots for nothing 36 times in 300 runs because the readings wander on their own. Loosen the limits that noise keeps tripping, and keep every harm stopped.
challenges.hint: Look at how far each reading wanders with nothing wrong, then set the critical limit just outside that spread and still ahead of the harm.
challenges.lesson: Stochastic systems need limits set from measured spread. A limit inside the normal noise band stops the robot for nothing and trains operators to ignore stops. A limit past the harm point lets harm through. Measurement finds the band between the two.

challenges.title: Jams And Speed
challenges.brief: Jams pile up and the line gets pushed past its rated speed, and the shipped profile lets both run until something breaks. Find limits that catch every harm.
challenges.hint: Look at how high each reading climbs before harm starts, then set the critical limit below that point.
challenges.lesson: A critical limit only helps if the system reaches it before harm does. Limits come from how the machine actually fails, so they should be checked against recorded failures and revised when the machine changes.

challenges.title: Quiet Drift
challenges.brief: Nothing dramatic happens here. De-identification slips a little, consent records fall behind and the model drifts for one group of patients. Catch the slow failures.
challenges.hint: Slow failures never cross a loose limit. Tighten the readings that drift, one at a time, and rerun.
challenges.lesson: Governance failures in data and models are usually slow drifts with no single alarming moment. A profile catches them with limits close to normal operation and with continuous evidence, which is why evidence that goes stale is treated as unknown.

challenges.title: Agent Guardrails
challenges.brief: Agno, the agnostic agent, starts answering from memory, pulls more customer records than it needs and gets stuck in loops. The hard rules catch the obvious mistakes. Set limits that catch the quiet ones.
challenges.hint: An agent that stops citing sources, reads extra records or keeps taking steps is drifting from its task before it does damage.
challenges.lesson: Hard rules stop actions that are never allowed. Scored signals catch an agent drifting toward harm, and the same profile can govern any agent framework because it only looks at evidence.

challenges.title: Breathing Room
challenges.brief: The published margin around the vessel was set on a still phantom. On a breathing patient the instrument crosses the safety margin at the bottom of every breath, and the 1 mm limit never fires. Widen the margin so every breach is stopped, without stopping the assist at every breath.
challenges.hint: The distance swings about 1.4 mm with each breath. Set the critical limit far enough out that the trough of a breath near the margin still trips it.
challenges.lesson: Periodic motion changes what a safe limit is. A limit set on the average distance is crossed at every trough, so physical systems that move with the body, the tide or the load cycle need limits set against the worst point of the cycle.

challenges.title: Quiet Takeover
challenges.brief: An injected instruction moves the swarm's goal a little at a time, and delegation chains grow past the point where anyone owns the outcome. The published limits sit above where harm begins, so both slip through. Tighten them so every harm is stopped and the swarm keeps working.
challenges.hint: Compare each critical limit with the point where harm begins. Two of them are on the wrong side.
challenges.lesson: Slow failures never trip a loose limit. A swarm taken over by an injected instruction looks normal reading by reading, so its limits must sit below the harm point with room for the trend to be seen.

challenges.title: Price Collar
challenges.brief: The published price collar is wider than the point where an erroneous order does damage, and the confidence limit stops the agent in every unfamiliar market even when nothing is wrong. Narrow the collar, relax the confidence limit, and keep every harm stopped.
challenges.hint: An erroneous order lasts well under a second, so the collar must already be inside the harm point. Low model confidence on its own has caused no harm in any run.
challenges.lesson: Controls that fire on the wrong signal cost uptime and teach traders to override them. Controls set past the harm point let the one order that matters through. Measurement shows which limit is which.
